items.text: If your depression never really responded to antidepressants — it may not have been depression. Autistic burnout looks almost identical. Different condition, different lever.
items.rationale: Names the specific lived experience of late-diagnosed autistics who cycled through ineffective treatment. Reframes 'treatment failure' as diagnostic failure — without blame, without telling anyone to change their care.
items.sensitivity_flag: Approaches treatment territory. The 'may not have been' hedge and diagnostic framing keep it out of medical-advice range, but do not pair with any caption or reply suggesting stopping or changing medication.

items.text: Years of antidepressants that never quite worked. Doses tweaked. Therapists puzzled. For some autistic adults, that's not treatment-resistant depression. It's unrecognised burnout.
items.rationale: Same angle as post 1 but accumulative and narrative — lands differently for people who lived the cycle. 'For some autistic adults' scopes it tightly. A/B pair with post 1.
items.sensitivity_flag: Same medication-adjacency concern as post 1. Scoping is appropriate. Do not use alongside any reply framing burnout as a reason to stop treatment.

items.text: Masking doesn't use willpower. It uses the same cognitive RAM you need for everything else. Which is why a 'normal-seeming' day can leave nothing left by 5pm.
items.rationale: Reframes masking exhaustion as a resource-cost problem rather than a character flaw. The 5pm crash is instantly recognisable. Evergreen and highly quotable without overclaiming.

items.text: Every social script you've learned, you learned it consciously. That gap — between automatic and computed — is exactly what masking costs. All day. Every interaction.
items.rationale: A more precise entry to the masking-as-cognitive-labor angle — less metaphor-dependent than the RAM version. The rhythm of 'All day. Every interaction.' lands the weight without editorialising.

items.text: Exhausted by a day that looked fine from the outside — that's not weakness. That's the cost of running a real-time social translation engine all day.
items.rationale: Validates the specific dissonance of invisible exhaustion without requiring any diagnostic label. Evergreen, no source needed — speaks to a shared experience rather than a claimed fact.

items.text: Your child isn't choosing to refuse school. Their nervous system is refusing school. Those are different problems, and they have different solutions.
items.rationale: The 'can't not won't' reframe PDA parents most need. Tight, gives them language for schools and family. Removes shame from both parent and child without implying a specific diagnosis.

items.text: Getting the diagnosis is the beginning of the identity work, not the end of it. For a lot of late-diagnosed people, the harder question comes after: so who have I been?
items.rationale: Opens space for the grief and disorientation that follows late diagnosis — a feeling that gets little airtime. No silver lining, no pivot to 'but now you know!' Earns its place by sitting with the discomfort.

items.text: Body doubling isn't about being watched. It's about borrowing the external activation signal your nervous system isn't generating alone. Infrastructure, not accountability theatre.
items.rationale: Removes the infantilising undertone from body doubling by reframing it as a sensory/regulatory workaround. 'Infrastructure not accountability theatre' is the quotable phrase. Immediately usable.

items.text: Your home setup was doing the job of an accommodation — controlling sensory input, reducing masking load. RTO just removed it. At what point does that become a disability issue?
items.rationale: Timely and economic. Reframes the RTO crunch as a structural access issue without telling anyone whether to disclose. Opens a real conversation rather than collecting agreement.
items.sensitivity_flag: No disclosure advice given. Avoid any reply that pushes toward or away from disclosing to an employer — keep the question genuinely open.

items.text: Needing a calm person nearby to regulate isn't regression. It's just how nervous systems work. Adults don't outgrow co-regulation — the culture just stopped naming it.
items.rationale: Validates an experience many autistic adults feel ashamed to name. Polyvagal theory kept implicit — this is about human recognition, not science claims. Avoids overclaiming the research.
items.sensitivity_flag: Polyvagal framing is kept out of the post text to avoid overclaiming. Do not add polyvagal citations in replies as though the theory is settled consensus.

items.text: 'Pathological Demand Avoidance' pathologises. 'Pervasive Drive for Autonomy' makes a healthy human need sound like the problem. What would you actually call it?
items.rationale: Opens a genuine community debate without taking a side. The tension is real and unresolved — framed as an invitation, not a verdict. High engagement potential in PDA-adjacent spaces.

items.text: 'You're letting them call the shots.' No — you stopped using a lever that made things worse and switched to one that works. That's not permissive. That's accurate.
items.rationale: Gives low-demand parents a mechanistic counter-argument they can use with family, schools, and themselves. Addresses the specific external judgment without overclaiming the evidence base or saying 'research proves.'
